name: Noni fruit extract

lead: Noni is a tropical fruit used traditionally in the Pacific and now sold as juice, supplements and in cosmetics as an antioxidant botanical.
Wikipedia reports no confirmed clinical efficacy for any use. Skin research is limited to cell studies.

paras: An anthraquinone from the fruit was reported to boost extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured fibroblasts; this has not been tested in people.
Anthraquinones can be harmful, and a 2024 review is cited as linking oral noni products to liver disease. The FDA issued a 2018 warning letter over drug claims.

lead: Noni fruit extract comes from Morinda citrifolia, a tropical shrub of the coffee family spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors. The pungent fruit was historically a famine food, and parts of the plant were used in Polynesian medicine as a tonic. Today it is sold as juice, powders, supplements and in cosmetics.[1]

The fruit contains anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids, scopoletin and other compounds.[1] Wikipedia states there is no confirmed evidence of clinical efficacy for any intended use, and a 2024 review is cited there linking noni products to liver disease risk.[1] In 2018 the US FDA issued a warning letter to a noni marketer for unapproved drug claims.[1]
Laboratory work has reported that an anthraquinone from noni induced extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts, but no trial of noni on skin appearance was identified.

paras: Reported constituents include anthraquinones, lignans, polysaccharides, flavonoids, iridoids, scopoletin and fatty acids.[1] A pharmacokinetic study used scopoletin as a marker of noni exposure and noted the lack of product standardisation.[2]

A 2005 study reported that an anthraquinone isolated from noni fruit induced extracellular matrix synthesis in normal human fibroblasts.[3] A formulation study combined noni and pandan leaf extracts as an anti-dandruff shampoo.[4]

Wikipedia notes that anthraquinones can be harmful and cites a 2024 review reporting a risk of liver disease from noni supplements and drinks; it also records a 2018 FDA warning letter to Hawaiian Organic Noni, LLC.[1]

No trials of noni on skin or appearance were found. A phase I study of noni in advanced cancer patients sought a maximum tolerated dose using quality-of-life measures,[5] a pharmacokinetic study examined scopoletin levels,[2] and a rat and human intervention study reported effects on hangover symptoms.[6] A registered study of an iridoid-enriched beverage examined skin autofluorescence as a marker of oxidative stress (NCT01597076, n=34).[7] A phase II prostate cancer trial was terminated after six participants.[8]
